chapter_theme: Want of understanding (அறிவின்மை) is the real poverty. The unlearned and the base cannot take in good counsel, show themselves for what they are among the learned, and set up petty assemblies of their own, while the learned keep silent before those who would not absorb what they say.
structure_note: The chapter opens by making understanding the true wealth (251) and explaining, as a fancy, why the learned are poor (252). It then shows the unlearned among the learned (253-254), the learned holding back their speech (255-256), and the base who cannot receive good words (257-260), with a run of similes: the pig's trough, charcoal washed in milk, the fly on dung.

251.reading: Lack of fine understanding is poverty and having it is great wealth; when one thinks about it, a eunuch who longs to be a woman will still put on the jewels that catch every eye.
251.nuance: The simile is left unexplained in the verse. Shanmuganar draws the conclusion that the wealth of the senseless is like the eunuch's jewels: an adornment on something that lacks the essential thing. Pope's heading puts it as 'mere externals are nothing'.

252.reading: If you would know why men of wide learning lose standing and suffer want: the ancient Lady of the Tongue lives with them, so the Lady of the Flower keeps away in a sulk.
252.nuance: A playful explanation (Mudaliar names the figure தற்குறிப்பேற்றம், an imputed cause), not a theology of fortune. Mudaliar offers two reasons for the quarrel: Lakshmi and Sarasvati are mother-in-law and daughter-in-law, or two women do not share one man in peace.

253.reading: One who scorned his father's urging to learn, not taking it as worth heeding, will grab a stick in anger when someone quietly holds out a written leaf to him before many people.
253.nuance: The anger is the unlearned man's shame turned outward: he cannot read the leaf in public. Mudaliar records other readings of the last line, one in which he laughs in contempt, one in which he makes a noise to slip away.

254.reading: When a man who grew up without learning enters among the wise, if he sits quietly it is as if a dog sat there, and if he speaks it is as if a dog barked.
254.nuance: Silence does not save him: Mudaliar allows மெல்ல இருப்பினும் to mean 'even if he sits with restraint', which makes the verse deny the unlearned any good way to be present.

255.reading: The low all go among the poets of petty, senseless assemblies and say things they never learned; but the worthy, even when asked, do not speak of what they have learned, knowing it would not be taken in.
255.nuance: Pope calls the assembly 'heterodox'; neither commentator says so. Mudaliar has it as an assembly not joined to understanding, and Shanmuganar's poets are false poets.

256.reading: The learned and eloquent hold back, afraid of a lapse, while others talk freely: on the palmyra the dry leaves rattle, but the green leaf never makes a sound.
256.nuance: Mudaliar notes the images answer the statements in reverse order (green leaf to the learned, dry leaves to the rest). Silence here signals life and fullness, noise dryness.

257.reading: Telling the way of virtue to people who do not know the good is like pressing sweet mango juice into a pig's trough; like a stake driven on a rock, it splits at the head and does not go into their ears.
257.nuance: Two similes for two failures: the teaching is wasted (the trough) and it cannot penetrate (the stake on rock). Pope's translation is missing for this quatrain, and Shanmuganar's commentary appears under 256.

258.reading: Charcoal washed in milk and dried for many days never turns white, and understanding will not enter a body that has not earned it, though you drive it in with a stick.
258.nuance: நோலா உடம்பு is the hinge. Both commentators take it as a body without merit from good deeds (Mudaliar: from a former birth, so without innate understanding); Pope reads 'undisciplined body', which moves the cause from past births to present discipline.

259.reading: Like the fly that will not settle on a flower pouring honey and fragrance but craves filth, those whose minds are set on low things get nothing from the clear, honeyed words of the worthy.
259.nuance: The fault is in desire, not capacity: the fly passes the flower by preference. Mudaliar notes that 'low things' is a polite way of naming filth.

260.reading: Because his heart kicks away the faultless, subtle teaching of the learned, the base man looks into the face of another like himself and sets up a petty assembly of his own.
260.nuance: The rejection breeds a rival: two of a kind confirm each other. Pope reads it as founding a sect; Mudaliar's கோட்டி is the talk given there, Shanmuganar's a platform speech.

links.note: Both call want of understanding the true poverty. Kural 841 adds that the world does not count other lack as lack; 251 adds the image of jewels on one who lacks the essential thing.
Both use a person lacking the marks of a sex to picture a lack that ornament cannot cover: the unlearned wanting to speak (Kural), the senseless rich in their jewels (here).
Both separate wealth from wisdom. The Kural states it as two natures of the world under fate; 252 makes a comic myth of the same fact, the two goddesses quarrelling.
252 explains in jest why Fortune avoids the learned; 266 turns on her and curses her for going to the base and leaving the good.
Both show the unlearned exposed in company. In the Kural his standing wilts as he speaks; here he is asked to read and answers with a stick.

Kural 403 says the unlearned are very good if they can stay silent before the learned; 254 says that even sitting quietly among the wise, such a man is a dog sitting there. Same situation, opposite verdict. The tension holds on Parimelazhagar's plain reading of 403 (silence keeps them from exposure and may lead them to learning), not if 403 is taken as irony.
Both make the fool's mere presence among the worthy a defilement: unwashed feet on a bed (Kural), a dog sitting among them (here).
Both tell those who speak well not to speak in a mean assembly. 255 adds the reason, that the hearers would not take the meaning in, and pictures the low talking freely there.
Both use சோர்வு for the lapse in speech to be guarded against. The Kural says it because gain and ruin come from speech; 256 shows the learned guarding against it by silence.
Good teaching spilt where it is wasted: nectar spilt in a dirty yard (Kural), mango juice pressed into a pig's trough (here).

Both say teaching cannot override what a person already is: in the Kural one's own understanding prevails over many books; here understanding cannot be driven into a body without merit. On the commentators' reading both rest on past deeds.
Both use புன்கோட்டி, the petty assembly. 255 shows the low talking in such assemblies; 260 shows how one is founded, by a man who rejects the learned and finds his like.

source_issues: Quatrain 256: Shanmuganar's field also holds the text of quatrain 257 and his commentary on it; 257's own Pope and Shanmuganar fields are not aligned, and Pope's translation of 257 was not found.
Quatrain 260: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.
